claims.claim: Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units via indexed bands and tenure security rather than a hard cap.
The instrument that helps incumbents most is most likely to harm households still outside the segment.
The 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance capped increases within existing tenancies but left initial rents unregulated.
Median SDU rent per square foot rose 3.1 percent in 2021–2023, exceeding general private rent growth of 1.7 percent.
Real rent burden worsened from 31 to 34 percent of income under the ordinance.
Second-generation rent controls show small or null effects on housing stock.
The long-run elasticity of SDU-type supply to controlled rents is estimated at 0.31 to 0.48.
A 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years.
A 15 percent cut in initial rents yields about $900 a month to incumbents but blocks 3,000 to 4,000 households a year from entering.
Berlin's experience shows listing supply contracted after rent controls and suppressed increases released above trend when the law fell.
Stable stock under the 2021 ordinance is an artifact of a non-binding instrument, not proof landlords will not exit.
The Landlords Association's exit threat is unproven because its compliance-cost figures rest on a self-reported survey with a 34 percent response rate.
A band-based cap on initial rents is defensible as rate-capping rather than confiscation, avoiding compensation and judicial-review exposure.
Tenants prioritize tenure security and faster public-housing offers over rent relief.
61 percent of surveyed tenants would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year tenure security, and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer.
Inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock a year, and a certifiable tenancy register would cost 40 to 60 staff-years.
Enforcement would miss the most exploited tenants, such as those without written agreements and newest arrivals.
Tightening must be sequenced: build the register and inspection capacity before binding the band.
Policy should tighten tenure and entry pricing rather than rent levels.

cites.sentence: Median SDU rent per square foot rose 3.1 percent in 2021–2023 under the ordinance, against general private rent growth of 1.7 percent, and real rent burden worsened from 31 to 34 percent of income [D2p2].
Mrs Wong's experience matches the aggregate: her landlord "still raises rent by whatever the market of desperate newcomers bears," and the ordinance "changed nothing she can see" [D4p1].
The 2021 instrument was second-generation by design, and second-generation controls show small or null effects on stock [D6p2]
— but they also leave the actual pain point, the initial rent, unregulated [D9p1].

The reviewed literature estimates the long-run elasticity of SDU-type supply to controlled rents at 0.31 to 0.48: a 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1].

The working paper's Hong Kong-like model is starker still: a 15 percent cut in initial rents yields about $900 a month to incumbents, against 3,000 to 4,000 households a year unable to enter the segment, mostly new arrivals and newly formed households [D6p4].
Those are precisely the households D1 identifies as the segment's core population [D1p2].

Berlin confirms the mechanism: initial-offer rents fell, listing supply contracted within a year, and when the law fell the suppressed increases released above the pre-cap trend line — the bill handed to those still outside [D7p1][D7p3].

Berlin confirms the mechanism: initial-offer rents fell, listing supply contracted within a year, and when the law fell the suppressed increases released above the pre-cap trend line — the bill handed to those still outside [D7p1][D7p3].
Mr Chan, who would gain $800 a month from a cap, already fears exactly this: he has watched two units on his floor "emptied and locked for a year" [D3p2].
The counter-argument — that the stable stock under the 2021 ordinance proves landlords will not exit [D2p1]
That stability is an artifact of a non-binding instrument [D12p2].
The Landlords Association's exit threat [D5p2]

should be discounted, but not dismissed: it concedes it has no data on members' actual margins, and its compliance-cost figures rest on a 210-member survey with a 34 percent response rate, self-reported [D5p3].
Mrs Wong's building, where four landlords treat units as their pension, suggests some owners would stay [D4p2]; the stairwell flats converted to storage suggest others would not [D4p3].
Mrs Wong's building, where four landlords treat units as their pension, suggests some owners would stay [D4p2]; the stairwell flats converted to storage suggest others would not [D4p3].
Counsel judges it defensible as rate-capping rather than confiscation, avoiding the compensation and judicial-review exposure a hard cap would invite [D9p1][D9p2].
Counsel judges it defensible as rate-capping rather than confiscation, avoiding the compensation and judicial-review exposure a hard cap would invite [D9p1][D9p2].
Mr Chan does not ask for rent relief; he asks for the queue, saying he would "accept any rent to leave" if waiting time fell to three years [D3p3].
The NGO survey confirms this revealed preference: 61 percent would trade a nominal increase for three-year tenure security, 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer [D11p1].
Tenure security is cheap to deliver and attacks the insecurity Mr Chan calls "the worst part" [D3p1].
Inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock a year, and a band-based cap requires a certifiable tenancy register costing 40 to 60 staff-years to stand up [D10p1].

Worse, the tenants least able to complain — those with no written agreement, like Mrs Wong [D4p1], and the newest arrivals — are exactly those enforcement would miss, so the most exploited tail is protected last [D10p2].
